title: WHO Surgical Safety Checklist
subtitle: Sign in, time out, sign out: what each item prevents

sources.title: WHO guidelines for safe surgery 2009: safe surgery saves lives

sources.org: Safe Surgery Saves Lives Study Group (New England Journal of Medicine)
sources.title: A surgical safety checklist to reduce morbidity and mortality in a global population

red_flags.text: Emergency cases, out-of-hours lists, list changes and staff handovers mid-case: the settings in which checklists are most often skipped and errors most often happen.
Laterality, multiple sites, or levels (spine, digits, teeth): wrong-site surgery risk.
A checklist read aloud while people keep working, or ticked without the team stopping: compliance on paper, not in practice.
Anyone in the room who feels unable to speak up. The checklist only works if the most junior person can stop the case.

do_now.text: SIGN IN, before induction of anaesthesia, with at least the anaesthetist and nurse: confirm patient identity, site, procedure and consent with the patient. Prevents wrong-patient and wrong-procedure surgery.
Sign in: is the site marked? Prevents wrong-side and wrong-site surgery, especially where laterality or level applies.
Sign in: anaesthesia machine and medication check complete, and pulse oximeter on and working. Prevents undetected hypoxaemia and equipment failure at induction.

Sign in: known allergy, difficult airway or aspiration risk with equipment and help available, and risk of more than 500 mL blood loss (7 mL/kg in children) with access and blood planned. Prevents anaphylaxis to a known allergen, airway disasters and unprepared haemorrhage.

assess.text: TIME OUT, before skin incision, with the whole team stopping: every member introduces themselves by name and role. Names make it easier to speak up and to direct a request in a crisis.
Time out: surgeon, anaesthetist and nurse verbally confirm patient, site and procedure once more. This is the last chance to catch an error made upstream.
Time out: has antibiotic prophylaxis been given in the appropriate window before incision? Prevents surgical site infection from mistimed or omitted prophylaxis.

Time out: anticipated critical events. Surgeon: critical or non-routine steps, duration, anticipated blood loss. Anaesthetist: patient-specific concerns. Nursing: sterility confirmed including indicator results, and equipment issues. Prevents surprises nobody prepared for.
Time out: is essential imaging displayed? Prevents operating on the wrong side or level from memory.

investigate.text: Audit checklist completion and quality, not just the presence of ticks. Observational audit of a sample of cases reveals whether the team actually pauses.
Review incidents and never events against the checklist: which item, if done properly, would have prevented it.

resuscitate.text: Adapt the checklist to local practice by adding items, but do not remove the core items.
In a true emergency, do an abbreviated but spoken sign in and time out: identity, procedure, allergy, blood, and antibiotics. Skipping it entirely is when errors cluster.

definitive.text: SIGN OUT, before the patient leaves theatre: the nurse confirms aloud the name of the procedure performed as recorded. Prevents an operative note and coding that do not match what was done.
Sign out: instrument, swab and needle counts are correct. Prevents retained foreign objects.
Sign out: specimen labelled, read aloud including the patient name. Prevents lost or mislabelled histology, which can mean a missed cancer or the wrong patient treated.
Sign out: any equipment problems to be addressed, and key concerns for recovery and management of this patient. Prevents faulty equipment reaching the next patient and an incomplete handover.
Implementation of the checklist across eight hospitals in high- and low-income settings was associated with substantial reductions in complications and deaths.

escalate.text: Any team member may halt the case if a checklist item is not satisfied. The operating surgeon and anaesthetist support that, every time.
Report near misses caught by the checklist through the incident system; they are the evidence that keeps it in use.
Persistent non-compliance by an individual is a clinical governance issue, escalated to the theatre lead.

notes: The checklist works through the conversation it forces, not the paper. A team that reads it aloud without stopping gets the paper and loses the benefit.
Each item maps to a known failure: wrong site, hypoxaemia, anaphylaxis, unprepared haemorrhage, infection, retained swab, lost specimen. Knowing which is which makes it harder to skip.
The introduction by name is not a courtesy. In a crisis, a request directed to a named person gets done faster than one directed to the room.
